n-step returns

TD(0) looks one reward ahead and then trusts its estimate. Monte Carlo looks all the way to the end. In between, an $n$-step method uses $n$ real rewards and then the estimate. A single knob, $n$, slides from one to the other, and the best setting is usually in the middle.

S&B Example 7.1: 19 states in a row, start in the middle, step left or right with probability ½. Leaving on the left pays $-1$, on the right $+1$, everything else $0$, $\gamma = 1$. True values run from $-0.9$ to $0.9$. Start from $V = 0$ and run one episode with $n = 1$, then with $n = 8$: the final reward reaches the last $n$ steps of the trail, not just the last one.

Which n is best?

RMS error over the 19 states, averaged over the first 10 episodes and 30 runs, for each $n$ and $\alpha$. S&B Figure 7.2 runs the same experiment with $n$ up to 512.

Neither extreme wins. $n = 1$ (TD(0)) learns slowly from one-step targets, very large $n$ is Monte Carlo with its noisy returns. Intermediate $n$ (around 4 to 8) gives the lowest error, at a moderate $\alpha$.

The maths

The $n$-step return adds $n$ discounted rewards and then the current estimate of where the agent ends up:

$$G_{t:t+n} = R_{t+1} + \gamma R_{t+2} + \dots + \gamma^{n-1} R_{t+n} + \gamma^{n}\, V(S_{t+n})$$

If the episode ends before $t + n$, the sum stops at $R_T$ and there is no $V$ term: $G_{t:t+n} = G_t$. So $n = 1$ gives the TD(0) target $R_{t+1} + \gamma V(S_{t+1})$, and $n \ge T - t$ gives the Monte Carlo return $G_t$.

The $n$-step TD update is the usual one with this target:

$$V(S_t) \leftarrow V(S_t) + \alpha\big[G_{t:t+n} - V(S_t)\big]$$

The target needs rewards up to $R_{t+n}$, so the update for $S_t$ happens $n$ steps late, at time $t + n$. At the end of the episode the remaining states are updated with shorter sums.

Why it works: write the true value the same way, $v_\pi(s) = \mathbb{E}_\pi[R_{t+1} + \dots + \gamma^{n-1} R_{t+n} + \gamma^n v_\pi(S_{t+n}) \mid S_t = s]$. Subtracting, the rewards cancel:

$$\mathbb{E}_\pi\big[G_{t:t+n} \mid S_t = s\big] - v_\pi(s) = \gamma^n\, \mathbb{E}_\pi\big[V(S_{t+n}) - v_\pi(S_{t+n}) \mid S_t = s\big]$$

So the worst error of the expected target is at most $\gamma^n$ times the worst error in $V$ (the error reduction property):

$$\max_s \Big|\mathbb{E}_\pi[G_{t:t+n} \mid S_t = s] - v_\pi(s)\Big| \le \gamma^n \max_s \big|V(s) - v_\pi(s)\big|$$

Larger $n$ shrinks the bias from bootstrapping, but adds more random rewards to each target, which adds variance. With $\gamma = 1$ the bound is not a contraction, yet episodes ending still pull the targets towards the truth.
